list.listitem: Limp is a common source of parental and physician concern. C
The majority of cases of limp are due to mild trauma and resolve without treatment. C
Differentiation between antalgic and non-antalgic gait is important. Rarely does non-antalgic gait require emergent evaluation and referral. C
Fractures, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and neoplastic processes require emergent orthopedic referral. C
Radiographs are recommended as the initial imaging study; consider ultrasound if initial radiographs are non-diagnostic. C

background.definition: A limp is any deviation from a normal age-related gait pattern.

list.listitem: No large population based incidence studies; the child with a limp is a frequent source of orthopedic consultation, though.
In one study of children presenting to the emergency room, the incidence of acute atraumatic limp was 1.8/1000.
Trauma: strains/sprains, fractures, dislocations, compartment syndrome, stress fracture
Atraumatic: leg length discrepancy (LLD), scoliosis

Infection: septic arthritis
Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common causative organisms Kingella kingae if under 12 months old Salmonella in children with sickle cell disease Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active adolescents or high risk individuals Due to vaccination, Haemophilus influenza is less common nowadays With hematogenous spread, S. aureus is the most common cause Streptococcus and Escherichia coli in infants
Infection: osteomyelitis
Immune mediated: toxic synovitis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, Lyme disease, idiopathic chondrolysis of the hip
Congenital: developmental dysplasia of the hip
Acquired: SCFE, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (LCPD), osteochondritis dissecans
Neurologic: cerebral palsy, myelomeningocele
Neoplastic: leukemia/lymphoma, Ewing's sarcoma, Osteosarcoma
Referred: discitis, psoas abscess, testicular torsion, appendicitis
Other: child abuse, vasoocclusive crisis (sickle cell disease), somatic syndrome (conversion disorder)
Normal gait consists of the stance phase in which the foot is in contact with the ground (62%) and the swing phase (38%), in which the foot is in the air.
Antalgic gait is a painful gait. To minimize the pain, the amount of time the affected limb spends in the stance phase decreases, and that spent in the swing phase increases.
Non-antalgic gait is a painless gait, and can manifest as an equinus (toe-walking), Trendelenburg, steppage, circumduction (vaulting) or stooping gait ().
Child with a limp and a focal exam: obtain anterioposterior and lateral radiographs of the involved area. C
Child with a limp and a non-focal exam: obtain radiographs of both of the entire lower extremities. C
Consider ultrasound if initial radiographs are non-diagnostic. C

Predictive factors used to distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip include an oral temperature >38.5°C, peripheral WBC count >12,000 mm3, ESR >40 mm/hr, CRP >2.0 mg/dL, and a strict refusal to bear weight on the affected limb (). B

Due to repetitive loading of the femoral neck. Can be either compression side (inferior-medial neck) or tension side (superior-lateral neck)
Fever, refusal to bear weight, painful joint motion, increased WBC, ESR, CRP
Low grade fever, painful joint motion, mildly increased WBC, ESR, CRP
Fever, refusal to bear weight, local tenderness/swelling, increased WBC, ESR, CRP
Morning pain, pain with inactivity, multiple joints common
Exposure to endemic area, target rash, knee most common
Most common in white males ages 4 to 10 years, hip and groin pain, decreased hip internal rotation, flattening and fragmentation of femoral head
Adolescent obese males, hip/groin pain, hip externally rotated, radiographic findings "Valgus" SCFE - female predominance, comorbid endocrine or metabolic disorders
Progressive pain, night pain, constitutional symptoms, increased ESR, CRP
Social risk factors, skin lesions (burns, contusions), injuries at different stages of healing , associated psychopathology
Pain in the posterior part of the heel, tenderness at the site of insertion of Achilles tendon
Unequal limb measurements, positive Galeazzi test (), radiographic measurement
Positive forward bending test, curvature of spine on radiographs
Sexually active, positive urethral cultures
Positive Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers in newborns, unable to fully adduct hips on older infants; ultrasound findings
Neurological deficits
Back pain, fever, elevated ESR, radiographs demonstrate narrowing of the intervertebral disc space
Knee pain, tenderness over the tibial tuberosity
Knee pain, tenderness over the inferior pole of the patella

list.listitem: Key elements of the history include any history of trauma, the nature and location of pain, and associated features (eg, fever, anorexia, weight loss). Also ask about: birth history, developmental/gait milestones, neurologic conditions.
Examine child and parents separately if concerns about secondary gain or non-accidental injury exist.
Examine child undressed through several gait cycles, systematically paying attention to each limb and joint. Running may help uncover subtle gait abnormalities.
Inspect and palpate both lower extremities identifying the site of maximal tenderness. Examine the joints for swelling and range of motion.
Perform a thorough hip exam in non-ambulatory children, and in children with thigh or knee pain.
A thorough spine, neurologic, and abdominal examination is essential when pain is difficult to localize. Consider testicular exam in the appropriate scenarios.
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease: most common in white males (male-to-female ratio is 3 to 4:1) age 3 to 12. Hip and groin pain, with decreased internal rotation of hip (see ).
SCFE: Most common in obese, adolescent males (male-to-female ratio is 1.7:1); peak age of diagnosis 12 to 13 years. Bilateral in 20 to 40 percent of cases. Hip and groin pain, hip externally rotated.
Leg length discrepancy: positive Galeazzi test ().
The most useful element of the history and physicial for the diagnosis of septic arthritis in children presenting with an atraumatic limp is the presence of joint tenderness (LR+ 11.4).
Femoral neck stress fracture (FNSF): athletes, malnutrition, eating disorders, endocrine or metabolic conditions, overuse
Child with a limp and a focal exam: obtain anterioposterior and lateral radiographs of the involved area.
Child with a limp and a non focal exam: obtain radiographs of both of the entire lower extremities.

When obtaining radiographs of the hip joint, frog leg lateral views should always be obtained. Initial radiographs in children with stress fractures, early LCPD, osteomyelitis, and septic arthritis may be normal.

Child with systemic symptoms or suspicion for infection, inflammation, or malignancy: obtain a CBC with differential, C-reactive protein (CRP), and ESR. ESR and CRP are better negative predictors than positive predictors of an infectious process. With an ESR <25 mm/hr or a CRP <1 mg/dL, the probability of not having septic arthritis is 85% and 87% respectively.

In a European series of 417 children admitted over an 8 year period with non-traumatic hip pain, transient synovitis was diagnosed in 383, septic arthritis in 1 and Lyme disease in 1 patient, with 32 undiagnosed.

Suspicion for an infectious process: obtain cultures from blood, bone (in case of osteomyelitis), and joint fluid (in case of septic arthritis). The joint fluid should be sent for gram stain, cell counts, and cultures. However, negative blood, bone, or joint fluid cultures do not rule out osteomyelitis or septic arthritis.
Legg-Calve-Perthes: radiographs reveal flattening and fragmentation of the femoral head ().

SCFE: The femoral head (ball) is displaced posteriorly and medially with step-off at the physeal plate () in most cases of SCFE; on anteroposterior radiographs of the femur there is a varus appearance. Less common is "valgus" SCFE, where the femoral head is displaced proximolateral; often missed on anteroposterior radiographs, but also on lateral radiographs, therefore 3D CT images are useful in establishing diagnosis.

Skeletal scintigraphy is helpful when the initial clinical exam and radiographs are inconclusive or MRI is not possible (eg, medical devices/implants unsafe for MRI use, sedation is unavailable). In the acute setting can help distinguish transient synovitis or septic arthritis from osteomyelitis.

Ultrasound of the hip should be obtained when there is a suspicion for an effusion. Ultrasound is highly sensitive for detecting effusions; however it can not distinguish between sterile, purulent, and hemorrhagic effusions. A systematic review identified a study with 127 patients that reported a LR+ of 8.4 and LR- of 0.2 for the diagnosis of septic arthritis in children presenting with an atraumatic limp.
CT is highly useful for visualizing cortical bone.

MRI is an excellent modality for visualizing medullary bone, soft tissues, joints, and cartilage. Consider in Femoral Neck Stress Fracture (FNSF) as these can be missed on radiographs. Order with gadolinium if suspecting inflammatory arthritis or MRI arthrogram after intra-articular administration of contrast to evaluate for acetabular labral tear.
Leukocytosis is neither sensitive nor specific for osteomyelitis or septic arthritis. Absence of leukocytosis does not rule out an infectious process.
Clinical rule has been developed in 168 patients and validated in a second group of 154 to predict likelihood of septic arthritis in children with hip pain.

Criteria: Predictive factors used to distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip include an oral temperature >38.5°C, peripheral WBC >12,000/mm3, ESR >40 mm/hr, CRP >2.0 mg/dL, and a strict refusal to bear weight on the affected limb ().
Criteria for septic knee arthritis has less clinical value, with the possibility that approximately 52% of cases could be missed.
Other research has found the predicted probability of septic arthritis to be 59% with a sensitivity of 20% when all five predictors were positive.
Septic arthritis has not been found in cases where all five predictors were negative.
Fever has been found to be the most significant predictor of septic arthritis.
Although more studies are needed, consider the use of point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) to assess for transient synovitis in children during emergency room evaluation
Obtain a detailed history and perform a thorough physical exam.
Identify the type of gait (antalgic vs non-antalgic) and attempt to localize the pathological area.
Obtain radiographs of the pathological area; obtain CBC with differential, ESR, and CRP in a systemically ill child or in a child with a suspicion for infection, inflammation, or malignancy.

See for when to consider referral to the emergency room.

cell.label: Child with a limp. Painful (antalgic) gait?
Fever, refusal to bear weight, or ill appearance?
CBC, ESR, CRP; hip ultrasound for effusion
cell.path: 2 or more of: temperature >38.5 °C, non–weight bearing, ESR >40 mm/h, WBC >12,000/mm³, CRP >2 mg/dL
Focal bone tenderness, or septic arthritis excluded

cell.label: Recent injury?
Night pain, weight loss, fatigue, bruising, or pallor?
Hip and knee X-ray (AP and frog-leg lateral)
cell.path: Normal, symptoms over 6 weeks or swollen joints

cell.label: Painless gait. Neurologic deficit (weakness, spasticity, abnormal reflexes)?
Visible structural problem?
Suspect septic arthritis. Urgent joint aspiration and orthopedic referral.
Suspect osteomyelitis. MRI.
Transient synovitis likely. NSAIDs, recheck in 24–48 hours.
X-ray. Fracture (including toddler's fracture), sprain or strain, foreign body.
Apophysitis (Sever disease, Osgood–Schlatter, Sinding-Larsen–Johansson), stress fracture, osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), accessory navicular.
Leukemia. Urgent hematology referral.
X-ray, then MRI. Bone tumor (osteoid osteoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma).
Non–weight bearing, same-day orthopedic referral.
Orthopedic referral.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) or Lyme arthritis. Rheumatology referral.
Cerebral palsy, neuropathy, Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, muscular dystrophy. Neurology referral.
Leg length discrepancy, scoliosis, clubfoot.
Hip X-ray. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), LCPD, SCFE.

footnotes.footnote: SCFE often presents with knee or thigh pain only; examine and image the hip.
A toddler's fracture may not show on the first X-ray.

feature.caption: Types and Clinical Features of Nonantalgic Gaits.

tr.td: When the affected limb is in the stance phase, and the unaffected limb is in the swing phase, the pelvis fails to remain in the neutral position and exhibits a downward tilt toward the unaffected side.
To clear the ground during the swing phase, the child flexes the hip and knee joint excessively.
To clear the ground in the swing phase, the child circumducts/ abducts the affected extremity, forming a semicircular arc.
Child walks with head and neck forward, flexion at the knees and hip.
